output.brief: The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level that the policy requires for nomination, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination rates (28.6% vs 28.2%), approval rates (73.8% vs 71.0%) and promotion rates (21.1% vs 20.0%) are nearly the same. Applying office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2% remote promotion, and the observed rate is 7.6%. Remote attrition is not higher. I'm fairly confident in this, with one caveat: only 110 remote employees are eligible, so a real difference of a few points can't be ruled out. The anecdotes about urgent work going to nearby staff suggest a possible visibility effect, but nothing measures it. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread comparison. Next: put the rule on hold, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Optionally, start tracking stretch-assignment allocation and explain the eligibility rules to remote staff.
